title: P1 Root Backend Performance
objective: Close P1 scalar-root backend and performance acceptance with a representative backend-neutral correctness/benchmark corpus, evidence-backed acceleration decision, honest budgets, and exact-candidate release qualification evidence

handoff.summary: Added a 12-case, five-sample backend-neutral scalar-root corpus spanning bisection, Brent, secant, and Newton, traced and untraced runs, and cheap/moderate/expensive callbacks. A dedicated adapter observes exact built Node, fresh npm, relocated SEA, real browser, and worker subjects; it independently checks roots, residuals, trace policy, method, and the ordinary-python backend. The exact-candidate collector binds the clean commit, runtime, source closure, corpus, adapter, capabilities, and artifacts. The backend survey retains ordinary CPython-parseable source: scalar iterations are sequential callback drivers, and no surveyed external/native option justifies callback crossings, payload, duplicated trace/resource semantics, and four-platform qualification. An authenticated Linux x64 Node 26.7.0 receipt for ec0f41497 passed all cases; median untraced solve time was 34.45-97.42 ms, traced Brent/secant/Newton was 102.93-120.01 ms, and traced bisection was 1.61-1.68 s.
risks: The authenticated receipt currently covers Linux x64 Node only. The hook supports npm, SEA, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, and the Chromium worker, but those exact artifact/runtime rows must be collected on the persistent release hosts before a cross-runtime or four-platform performance claim.

Traced bisection intentionally emits many teaching events and is substantially slower than the other methods. Its provisional 5000 ms/solve release ceiling is honest but loose; receipts expose the actual distribution and should be used to decide whether trace representation merits a separate optimization project.

The callback tiers are deterministic scalar functions, not vectorized batches, arbitrary ill-conditioned problems, cross-language callback bridges, cold startup, or UI latency. The documentation explicitly limits the conclusion to this envelope.
next_steps: Collect and retain exact-candidate npm, SEA, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, and Chromium-worker receipts using the common preparers and this collector during final numerical release qualification.
Run the same exact corpus on Linux ARM64, macOS ARM64, and Windows x64 before tightening provisional release ceilings or claiming platform-wide performance.

Revisit source-transparent acceleration only if a new representative corpus proves solver bookkeeping dominates callback work; do not add a separate C/Wasm scalar-root loop without end-to-end evidence and trace/resource parity.
